newsitem.title: USA: Titanium tightness to ease after Commerce ruling.
newsitem.headline: Titanium tightness to ease after Commerce ruling.

text.p: Russian titanium supplies to the United States, the world's biggest user of the light metal, are set to rise following a U.S. Commerce ruling which lowers dumping duties on imported product.
U.S. Commerce, in a final determination, said New York trader Interlink should face no dumping duty on the sponge, an intermediate product it imports from Russia's AVISMA producer into the U.S.
Commerce also confirmed a final dumping duty of 28.31 percent on imports by trader Cometals, down from a preliminary 89.9 percent duty.
The regular import duty of 15 percent on sponge imports from any country is still in force.
Andrew Mestel, Interlink's managing director, said imports of sponge into the U.S. from AVISMA will resume in the near future once U.S. Customs have been informed by Commerce.
"There are a number of consumers in the U.S. It's good news for us and good news for Russia," Mestel said.
"Most people would say the market is tight and interest in material is very strong. This will help loosen it up a bit," Mestel said.
Sponge in the U.S. is over $4 per pound, Mestel said.
Although most sponge imported to the U.S. comes from Japan, Mestel does not think overall level of imports will rise that much in the wake of Commerce's decision.
Russian material, which has been going to Japan, will now come to the U.S., while Japan will consume more of its own production domestically, Mestel said.
But Commerce's decision left Cometals, part of Commercial Metals Co, furious because it confirms different duties on product imported from AVISMA, Russia's sole sponge maker.
"What Commerce signifies is that they want only a single channel to bring material to the U.S.. It's totally absurd," said Joseph Lonner, Cometals president.
Lonner said Cometals is only able to import very limited quantities of Russian sponge because of the duty. "We are not competitive," he added.

The U.S. has the largest titanium industry in the world with sales to the airline manufacturers dominating offtake. All of U.S. titanium's Big Three - Titanium Metals, RMI, and Oremet, or Oregon Metallurgical have to buy some sponge on the open market to melt into ingot and billet for making products.
And more sponge will be needed because of a surge in aircraft orders.
Commerce's decision will benefit RMI in particular because it has no sponge making capacity of its own, and had been lobbying the government to scrap dumping duties.
"We have a good relationship with all of the consumers of Russian sponge in the U.S.," Mestel said.

Joe Compofelice, chief financial officer of Timet's parent, Tremont Corp, said Commerce's decision will have little effect on his company because its European operations were able to buy Russian sponge in Europe and melt it there to make ingot or billet.
"But it's no longer a disadvantage to RMI and Oremet. The playing field is now level as long as the Russians continue to sell it at a fair price," said Compofelice.
-- Huw Jones, New York Commodities 212-859-1646
